adversarial_test_results.prompt:
FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present disclosure relates generally to methods of depositing thin films on semiconductor substrates, and more particularly to methods of controlling the composition and density of dielectric films deposited by atomic layer deposition.

BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

As semiconductor devices shrink, the thickness of the gate dielectric and the uniformity of that thickness become increasingly important. A film that is too thin may leak current, while a film that is too thick may slow the switching of a transistor. Manufacturers therefore require processes in which the deposition rate is stable and the distribution of the film across the wafer is uniform. Previous approaches have used thermal oxidation, chemical vapour deposition and sputtering, but each of these methods has drawbacks. Thermal oxidation consumes silicon from the substrate, chemical vapour deposition often produces films with a high concentration of hydrogen, and sputtering can damage the underlying structures. Atomic layer deposition avoids these problems because the reaction is self-limiting, so the growth rate per cycle depends only on the chemistry of the surface.

SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

In one aspect, a method comprises exposing a substrate to a first precursor, purging the chamber, exposing the substrate to a second precursor, and repeating these steps until a film of a desired thickness is obtained. The first precursor may be a metal halide, and the second precursor may be an oxygen source such as water, ozone or an oxygen plasma. The temperature of the substrate is maintained between about 200 and about 450 degrees Celsius, and the pressure of the chamber is maintained between about 0.1 and about 10 Torr. The composition of the resulting film can be tuned by varying the ratio of the purge time to the pulse time, and the density of the film increases as the deposition temperature rises.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION

The inventors have discovered that the properties of the deposited film depend on several process parameters. In a series of experiments, films were deposited on silicon wafers at temperatures ranging from 200 to 450 degrees Celsius, and the thickness of each film was measured by ellipsometry. The refractive index of the films increased with temperature, which indicates that the films became denser as the temperature rose. The concentration of carbon in the films fell sharply above 300 degrees Celsius, while the concentration of oxygen remained nearly constant. The ratio of oxygen to metal in the films approached the stoichiometric value at the highest temperatures studied.

The structure of the deposited films was examined by X-ray diffraction. Films deposited at low temperature were amorphous, whereas films deposited at high temperature showed weak diffraction peaks. The symmetry of the crystal lattice was found to depend on the partial pressure of the oxygen source: higher partial pressures favoured a cubic arrangement, while lower partial pressures produced a mixture of phases. The distribution of grain sizes through the thickness of the film was also measured, and a strong correlation between grain size and leakage current was observed.

In a further embodiment, the film is annealed at a temperature between about 500 and about 700 degrees Celsius for between about 10 and about 60 minutes. Annealing reduces the concentration of hydroxyl groups and improves the electrical properties of the film. As for the choice of ambient gas during annealing, nitrogen is preferred because it is inexpensive and unreactive. The leakage current of capacitors formed from the annealed films was below about 10^-8 amperes per square centimetre at an applied voltage of one volt. These results demonstrate that the composition, structure and density of the film can be controlled independently by appropriate selection of the deposition and annealing conditions.
